transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-03-15
Start: 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Jamie Liu (Redwood AE), Ravi Menon (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Argent SRE), Luis Ortega (Argent ML Eng), Hannah Kim (Argent CTO)

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive on KV cache eviction, paging behavior with long-context sessions, and prefix reuse patterns observed by Argent. Goal: reproduce eviction, propose mitigations (config, runtime, dedicated), and scope bench runs.

Transcript:
00:00 Jamie Liu: hey everyone thanks for joining, we got about an hour 15, uh we'll focus on the kv cache symptoms you reported. can someone summarize the prod behaviour again?
00:18 Maya Patel: yeah so since we started opening long sessions for a single user 
 think multi-turn support where we stitch in person state 
 we see more frequent token generation stalls and sometimes completions that restart or repeat, and our ops logs show frequent KV eviction events, like key eviction on worker-2, worker-4.. it's noisy.
00:34 Ravi Menon: when you say eviction, is that the runtime eviction (in-memory kv) or are you seeing paging to disk?
00:40 Maya Patel: primarily eviction from GPU memory, then we get paging logs in host side; we aren't fully paging to disk but we see the runtime moving older KV segments out to host and that increases latency a lot.
00:51 Luis Ortega: also we noticed prefix reuse patterns 
 many sessions share a long system/prompt prefix reused across users, so the cache keeps hot prefixes but then per-user tails are unique, there's a lot of fragmentation.
01:10 Jamie Liu: cool ok so sounds like three things: long-context causing large kv state, prefix reuse leading to hot entries blocking space for unique tails, and fallback/paging paths that add latency. we'll walk through runtime counters and config knobs.
01:28 Ravi Menon: quick note on terminology 
 our 'KV cache' is the per-shard key/value store for attention states; eviction happens when we exceed per-GPU reserved KV budget or when the worker needs to free space for new sequences. the runtime supports paging to host memory and an LRU-like eviction but it's approximate 
 with very long prefix reuse you can get cache churn.
01:47 Hannah Kim: is there an upper bound we can tune? like pinning the prefix so it never evicts?
01:55 Ravi Menon: yes we can pin certain prefixes or session ids. we expose a 'pin' API in the runtime and also a 'session affinity' routing so the same worker keeps the cache for the session. both help but have tradeoffs in capacity efficiency.
02:13 Maya Patel: can you explain session affinity more? we tried sticky routing but it seemed to still evict after 10k tokens.
02:21 Ravi Menon: session affinity only reduces cross-worker duplication; if a worker's total KV footprint exceeds the device budget it will still evict. so affinity plus pinning helps for inter-worker reuse, but you may still need to increase per-worker kv budget or add more workers/pool size.
03:05 Luis Ortega: we run a 2x accel config (A100-ish profile) with 40B model, quantized to int8, and we saw eviction rates spike when we cross ~1.5M context tokens active. below that it's stable. once we go over it, eviction frequency increases nonlinearly.
03:28 Ravi Menon: that tracks; kernel selection and kv storage for int8 are smaller but the attention states still scale with seq_len * layers. paging thresholds are heuristic right now.
03:40 Jamie Liu: two practical axes to consider: 1) decrease runtime pressure (batching, prefix dedupe, pinning), 2) improve capacity (dedicated capacity, different quantization profiles, increase kv per-GPU), and 3) change routing policies (spillover to other pools or colder storage).
04:05 Maya Patel: more detail on prefix dedupe? how do we detect identical prefix tokens efficiently?
04:12 Ravi Menon: we use a lightweight fingerprint (rolling hash) on prefix token ids; if the fingerprint matches a cached entry we reuse the cached KV tensors; the issue is when prefixes are semantically identical but tokenized differently (minor whitespace changes), or when you glue session-specific metadata onto the front, the fingerprints differ and we miss reuse.
04:40 Luis Ortega: so canonization could help 
 strip certain metadata or normalize whitespace before tokenization. but our product team wants to keep user-specific identifiers in the prompt, so we need a hybrid approach.
04:58 Jamie Liu: recommended approach: canonicalize stable parts of prefix (system instructions, app state), then attach user-specific tokens after a separator. also expose an explicit cache key API so you can declare which prefix should be deduped.
05:20 Hannah Kim: what about eviction policy? LRU seems naive for our workload. can we favor pinned prefixes and prefer dropping tails?
05:29 Ravi Menon: yes we have an eviction weight policy; pinned keys get infinite weight, you can set weights per key, and we try to evict lowest weight first. but when many unique tails exist across users, total entropy defeats weights. also note that we evict at tensor-block granularity (per-layer KV chunks) not per-token.
06:02 Maya Patel: the logs we sent show eviction events correlated with batching spikes. sometimes when we get a sudden burst of batched requests the worker tries to allocate for the batch and evicts aggressively. is there a graceful fallback?
06:18 Ravi Menon: runtime will attempt to either reduce batch size (if auto-batching enabled) or spill to host for some KV objects. There's also a config to prefer reducing throughput (queuing) rather than evicting 
 tradeoff latency vs correctness. we can tune that knob for you.
06:38 Jamie Liu: for the bench we want to reproduce: a steady state of many concurrent sessions with reuse of a long shared prefix + unique tails, and intermittent bursts. we'll set up a soak test with 500 concurrent sessions, average 20 requests per session, and total active token horizon up to 2M.
07:02 Luis Ortega: can we instrument per-layer eviction counts? we want to know which layers are dominating KV size.
07:08 Ravi Menon: yes we can produce per-layer counters and heatmaps. I can attach the dump 
 shows top-k layers for evictions and tensor sizes.
07:25 Hannah Kim: one more related topic: quantization. does using int8 vs int4 change eviction behaviour? smaller model weight isn't same as smaller KV, right?
07:35 Ravi Menon: correct. quantization reduces model parameter memory but KV cache (attention states) are typically stored in fp16 or bf16 for numerical stability; we do support compressed KV (e.g., fp16->int8 packed), but that adds CPU/GPU decompression cost. In practice int8 weights reduce base memory, letting you allocate slightly more KV before eviction, but compressing KV is the biggest win if you can accept extra latency.
08:05 Maya Patel: do you recommend dedicated capacity for us? we have predictable traffic but high long-context tail.
08:12 Jamie Liu: Dedicated helps because you can increase per-GPU KV budgets and control routing; plus SLA prevents noisy neighbor evictions. For long-context heavy workloads dedicated is common. But first let's try software mitigations to quantify remaining need.
08:28 Luis Ortega: what's the impact of prefix pinning on cost? it sounds like pinning many prefixes will blow up memory use.
08:35 Ravi Menon: exactly. pinning is effective for a small set of very hot prefixes (shared system prompts). We recommend pinning only canonical app-level prefixes, not per-user ones. Also, combine pinning with session affinity to reduce duplication across workers.
09:02 Maya Patel: we sent a snippet of our runtime logs showing 'kv_evict: key=0x7f... layer=23 size=... reason=alloc' 
 can you interpret that?
09:12 Ravi Menon: 'reason=alloc' means the worker tried to allocate a new KV tensor and freed older blocks to make room. The layer number helps see whether mid vs top layers are evicted. typically top layers are larger; if you see lower layer evictions it suggests fragmentation or many short-lived keys.
09:34 Jamie Liu: quick interjection: sometimes third-party tokenizers change tokenization between SDK versions and that causes missed cache hits. please log tokenizer+vocab hash in the session metadata.
09:50 Luis Ortega: noted. we'll add tokenizer hash.
10:00 Jamie Liu: let's talk paging thresholds 
 currently runtime uses a soft limit at 70% device KV budget to start paging to host to avoid hard evicts; any reason you'd prefer more aggressive paging vs eviction?
10:14 Maya Patel: paging lowers p99 by a lot relative to eviction? it seems paging still good but not as bad as a full recompile. we saw ~200ms added for some hot tails but eviction led to repeated recompute and bigger delays.
10:28 Ravi Menon: yes paging is preferable for latency continuity, but if host memory isn't colocated you'll still pay a penalty. Also repeated page-in/out churn can be worse than strategic evict-and-recompute for some workflows. We can tune the 'start_paging_at' % and per-key pin thresholds.
11:02 Luis Ortega: are there any heuristics to prioritize keeping keys that are more likely to be reused soon? like recency vs frequency weighted by session affinity?
11:12 Ravi Menon: we have a recency-frequency hybrid and you can inject custom reuse hints from your app (e.g. set reuse_score for a key when you know it's likely to be hit). That API is often under-used.
11:30 Hannah Kim: how about saving KV to NVM or fast SSD as a cold tier for very long contexts?
11:36 Ravi Menon: long-term cold tier is possible but expensive; restore latency from SSD is high compared to host memory; best for very large dormant sessions where immediate latency isn't required. For your interactive use-case host paging is usually enough.
12:10 Jamie Liu: let's outline the short-term plan: 1) Ravi will send per-layer eviction heatmaps and logs; 2) Argent will add tokenizer/hash and sample payloads; 3) run a bench with pinned shared prefixes and session-affinity enabled to measure delta; 4) decide on dedicated pilot if software mitigations don't hit SLA.
12:42 Maya Patel: sounds good. one more ask: can we get a recommended runtime.conf for our workload? like suggested kv_budget, start_paging_at, pin_keys config.
12:51 Ravi Menon: yes I'll include a tuned runtime.conf with comments. it'll have conservative defaults and an aggressive variant for the bench.
13:05 Jamie Liu: ok let's jump into the logs Ravi attached (link shared in chat).
13:12 Ravi Menon: (screen-sharing) here's the eviction timeline: you can see a sharp increase at t=2h30 in the soak where active token count crosses 1.5M. layers 20-24 show the most evictions. also note that LRU timestamps show many small keys evicted rather than large chunk evictions -> fragmentation.
14:10 Luis Ortega: fragmentation 
 does compaction exist? like periodic defragmentation?
14:18 Ravi Menon: we do a lazy compaction during low load windows; there's also an admin-triggered compaction. compaction costs GPU cycles and is best scheduled during low traffic. We can propose midnight compaction windows.
14:45 Maya Patel: what's the expected p95/p99 hit if we enable compressed KV?
14:52 Ravi Menon: compressed KV adds ~20-60ms decompression on access depending on layer and compression format, but it can reduce overall eviction frequency by 40-60% in tests. So p99 might improve because fewer hard evictions occur, even though individual accesses might add small CPU/GPU cost.
15:25 Hannah Kim: any security implications with paging to host or SSD? we need audit logs and encryption for private deployment.
15:32 Jamie Liu: Redwood Private supports host-side encryption and integrates with KMS/HSM; audit logs for eviction/paging events can be exported to your SIEM. We'll include the architecture and network diagrams in the SOC2 pack.
15:50 Maya Patel: perfect. also curious about metrics 
 what should we monitor to detect impending eviction?
15:58 Ravi Menon: key metrics: device_kv_utilization_pct, active_token_horizon, per-worker_eviction_rate, avg_batch_alloc_size, paging_rate. Alerts on device_kv_utilization > 65% sustained are a good early warning.
16:20 Luis Ortega: and what about batching? you mentioned auto-reduce batch size to avoid eviction; is that available now?
16:27 Ravi Menon: yes auto-batching has a throttle mode that reduces new batch formation when memory pressure spikes, trading throughput for latency stability. We'll enable it for the bench.
16:42 Jamie Liu: ok wrapping toward next steps 
 anything else from Argent?
16:46 Maya Patel: no, just that we'll prioritize sharing payloads and enabling sampler in next 48 hours.
16:52 Hannah Kim: we'll also decide if we want a dedicated pilot based on bench results.
17:00 Jamie Liu: perfect. thanks everyone. we'll send notes, runtime.conf, SOC2, bench plan.
17:10 -- End of meeting --
